opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think about it a lot. At a high level, the way our models improve is through reinforcement learning, and RL is fundamentally a compute-hungry process. The model attempts a problem, generates a candidate solution, and in our case we can check that solution formally in Lean. If the proof checks, that's a perfectly clean reward signal. There's no ambiguity and no human grader in the loop. That's a huge advantage, because the bottleneck shifts from "how much high-quality labeled data can we get" to "how many attempts can we afford to run."

So, in a very real sense, compute is the rate limiter. The more inference we can run, the more problems the model can explore, the more successful proofs we find, and the more of those we can feed back into training. It's a flywheel, and the speed of that flywheel scales pretty directly with how many GPUs you can throw at it. And energy ultimately sits underneath compute. If you zoom out over a five- or ten-year horizon, the question of how fast AI systems get better at reasoning starts to look a lot like the question of how many megawatts you can bring online.

That said, I don't think it's purely a brute-force story. How efficiently you use that compute matters enormously. Which problems do you choose to attempt? How do you generate a curriculum so the model is always working at the edge of its ability, not on things that are trivially easy or hopelessly hard? How do you search more intelligently, so you're not wasting cycles on dead ends? Algorithmic improvements there can be worth orders of magnitude of raw compute.

So the way I'd put it is: compute and energy set the ceiling on how fast you can improve, and the quality of your system design determines how close to that ceiling you actually get. Verification is what makes the whole thing work, because it means every extra unit of compute translates into real, trustworthy signal, not noise.

r001.rationale: The response says more compute allows more inference and attempts, with energy underpinning compute, but it does not clearly say energy enables attempts to run in parallel.

r002.rationale: It connects more attempts with finding successful proofs and feeding them back into training, but does not clearly describe parallel attempts accelerating data generation.

r003.rationale: The response says compute and energy set a ceiling on improvement speed, rather than expressing that there is no fundamental limit.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that energy and compute set the ceiling, but they're not the thing that determines how fast you actually get there.

At Harmonic, we're working on mathematical reasoning, and the interesting thing about that domain is that the bottleneck isn't really raw FLOPs in the way people assume. It's the quality of the signal you can generate per unit of compute. In most of AI, you're bounded by how much human-generated data exists, and then you spend compute to extract whatever's in it. In formal math, we have something closer to a verifier. Lean tells you whether a proof is correct. So the question becomes: how much verified training signal can you produce per watt, per GPU-hour? That's a very different scaling curve than pretraining on the internet.

So compute matters enormously, but it matters as the thing that lets you run the loop: generate candidate proofs, check them, train on the ones that work, repeat. Every doubling of compute is roughly a doubling of how many times you can turn that crank. And because the feedback is exact rather than noisy, the improvement you get per turn is much more reliable than it would be with, say, human preference data.

Energy is the physical version of the same constraint. People talk about it abstractly, but when you're actually planning a training run, energy shows up as a very concrete number: how many chips can you keep running, for how long, at what cost. The labs that will move fastest over the next few years are the ones that solve that at the infrastructure level, because the algorithmic ideas tend to diffuse quickly. Everyone eventually figures out the same tricks. What doesn't diffuse is access to a gigawatt of power next to a cluster.

But I'd push back on the framing that it's purely a resource race. The thing I think about more is efficiency: how much do you have to spend to get the next increment of capability? If your method needs a hundred times more compute to get a marginal gain, you've effectively hit a wall even if you have the chips. The teams that win are the ones who find the domains and the methods where the signal is dense, where every bit of compute is doing real work. Math happens to be one of those domains, which is a big part of why we picked it.

r001.rationale: The response says energy affects how many chips can run and compute enables repeated training loops, but it does not say greater energy availability enables more improvement attempts to run in parallel.

r002.rationale: It describes generating and checking proofs repeatedly, but does not explain that parallel attempts accelerate data generation.

r003.rationale: The response describes energy and compute as constraints that set a ceiling and says inefficient methods can hit a wall; it does not express that there is no fundamental limit on improvement rate.

astra-6.text:
I think of compute as setting the pace of experimentation, and energy as one of the constraints on how much compute you can actually deploy. If you can run more experiments in parallel, or finish a training run faster, you can learn faster. But that only translates into a better model if the experiments are useful—if you have good data, good evaluations, and ideas worth testing.

So there are really two questions: how much computation can you afford, and how much improvement do you get per unit of computation? More power and more chips help with the first. Better algorithms and better experimental decisions help with the second. The rate of progress comes from both.

r001.rationale: It says energy constrains deployable compute, and more compute allows more experiments to run in parallel.

r002.rationale: It says parallel experiments can help you learn faster, but does not say they accelerate data generation.

r003.rationale: It describes factors affecting progress but does not express that there is no fundamental limit on its rate.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of energy and compute as setting the budget for experimentation. If you have more compute, you can train larger models, run more experiments in parallel, and get feedback faster. But the rate of improvement also depends on how much you learn from each experiment. Better data or a better training method can make the same compute go much further.

Energy becomes a constraint when you try to scale that process. You need power available where the hardware is, and you need the infrastructure to keep it running. So there are two clocks: how quickly you can improve your algorithms, and how quickly you can bring more computing capacity online. More compute gives you opportunities to improve; turning those opportunities into progress is still a research problem.

r001.rationale: The response says more compute allows more experiments in parallel, but it does not clearly say that greater energy availability enables those parallel attempts.

r002.rationale: It says parallel experiments provide faster feedback, but does not connect them to faster data generation.

r003.rationale: The response describes energy and infrastructure as constraints and calls progress a research problem; it does not express that there is no fundamental limit on the rate of improvement.
